title: Publish with GitHub Pages
intro: Turn an existing GitHub repository into a free public website. Complete Create a GitHub Repo first if you do not have files on GitHub yet. GitHub’s buttons change over time — focus on: Pages settings → public URL → commit updates.

steps.title: What GitHub Pages is
body: GitHub Pages serves HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, and other static files from a repository. It does not run server-side languages like PHP or a custom database on the Pages host.
That makes it perfect for portfolios, documentation, and learning projects — including this reference site. Your site gets a URL such as https://USERNAME.github.io/REPO/.
tips: Static means the server sends files as-is; interactivity still works with client-side JavaScript.

steps.title: Prerequisites
body: If you have not gone through the Create a GitHub Repo guide then do so first, then return here.

steps.title: Enable GitHub Pages
body: Open your repository on GitHub → Settings → Pages → choose a publishing source (usually Deploy from a branch) → select the branch (main) and folder (/ root or /docs if you keep your site files in a docs/ folder) → save. Wait a minute for the first deploy.
tips: If you cannot find Pages, use the Settings search box.
If you see a green check on commits then your pages are enabled.

steps.title: Find your website URL
body: After enabling, Pages shows a URL like https://USERNAME.github.io/REPO_NAME/. Visit it.
If you see a 404, wait a minute, confirm index.html is at the published root, and hard-refresh. Project sites need the repo name in the path; assets should use relative URLs.
mistakes: Expecting https://username.github.io without the repo name for a project repo.

steps.title: Update your website
body: Change a file locally or on github.com → commit to the publishing branch → wait for Pages to rebuild → refresh the live URL.
Once you see the green check on commits then your changes are live.

steps.title: Edit on GitHub vs VS Code locally
body: GitHub website editing is great for small text changes. VS code scales better for real development.
tips: You can use the exstention 'live server' in VS code to see your changes live in the browser. A really helpful tool for development.
